Rate the following clinical vignette:

Vignette: Hemi

Hemi is a 71-year-old Māori man who has been married to his wife, Aroha, for nearly forty-five years. He works part-time as a cashier at a large supermarket near his home in South Auckland — a job he took on after retiring from construction work, partly to stay busy, partly because he genuinely enjoys talking to people. Or he used to.

About two years ago, Hemi was finishing an evening shift when a young man entered the store and attacked another customer — a woman in her mid-thirties — with a knife, just three registers down from where Hemi was standing. He watched the whole thing unfold in the space of perhaps thirty seconds. He remembers the sound more than anything else: the woman's scream cutting off too quickly, the wet noise he cannot bring himself to describe even now, the way his own voice disappeared when he tried to call out. He was frozen behind his register, hands flat on the counter, unable to move until a colleague pulled him into the back room. The woman survived, but only just.

In the weeks that followed, Hemi told himself he was fine. He is not a man who has ever considered himself fragile. He went back to work after a few days, stood behind his register, and smiled at customers. But something had shifted in a way he could not name at the time. He began scanning every person who walked through the automatic doors — reading their hands, their body language, the shape of their jackets. If someone moved quickly or reached into a bag, his heart would slam against his ribs and he would find himself gripping the counter again, back in that moment, smelling the blood he is certain he could smell even from three registers away.

He stopped sleeping well almost immediately. He lies awake most nights running through what he should have done — shouted a warning, moved toward her, done something — even though he knows, on some level, that there was nothing to be done. When he does sleep, he wakes from dreams he cannot fully recall but that leave him drenched and rigid beside Aroha, who has learned not to touch him suddenly in the night.

Hemi has become quieter at home. His grandchildren visit on weekends, and he loves them fiercely, but he finds the noise and chaos of a full house overwhelming in a way it never used to be. He sits apart more often now, watching from the edges. Aroha has noticed. She is a patient woman, but she tells him she misses him — that he is present in the room but somewhere else entirely, and she doesn't know how to reach him.

At work, he has requested a register near the back of the store, away from the entrance. His manager accommodated this without asking questions, and Hemi is grateful for that small mercy. Still, there are days when a particular sound — a shopping basket dropped on the floor, a child shrieking with laughter — will send him somewhere he doesn't want to go, and he has to excuse himself to the stockroom and breathe until the world stops narrowing. He has not told his colleagues why.

He carries a particular kind of shame about all of this. He is a grandfather, a husband, a man who spent decades doing physical labor without complaint. He did not experience the trauma himself — he was not the one who was hurt — and this distinction matters enormously to him, even as it provides no relief. He finds himself thinking about the woman sometimes, wondering whether she still carries it too, whether she knows that a man three registers away has not stopped seeing her fall.

He came to therapy at Aroha's quiet insistence. He sat in the first session with his hands on his knees and said, carefully, that he wasn't sure he deserved to be there.
